title: Bandwidth RoSetta: responsiveness scan and cost tradeoff
body:
Summary:
This is a working draft of a short benchmark comparing responsiveness (p50/p95) vs incremental $/1k-token cost across varied egress bandwidth and request burst shapes. Motivated by customer questions about: does higher network bandwidth materially reduce tail latency when using Redwood runtime features (KV cache + opportunistic prefetch) and how that maps to per-token cost under different batching strategies.

High-level takeaways (quick):
- Small steady traffic (sustained 50 qps): network bandwidth above 200 Mbps yields diminishing returns on p95 for our test models; batching + KV cache dominate improvements.
- Microbursts (20–200 qps spikes, 500ms duration): higher bandwidth (1 Gbps) reduces p95 by 18–30% vs 200 Mbps for H100-backed instances, but cost per 1k tokens increases slightly because faster responses reduce batching opportunities.
- Prefetch turned on (predictive prefix prefetch) reduces p95 consistently across bandwidth tiers and recovers most gains you'd expect from raw bandwidth increases — suggests software knobs are more cost-effective than pure egress upgrades.

Testbed & methodology (short):
- Model: open-llama-7B (quantized int8) served on dedicated Redwood pool.
- Hardware: H100 (80GB) baseline; A100 (40GB) for a subset of runs.
- Runtime config: default Redwood runtime with continuous batching enabled; we test three batching targets: small (max batch 8, latency-optimized), medium (max batch 32), large (max batch 128, throughput-optimized).
- KV cache: enabled in all tests; prefetch: toggled on/off.
- Network egress simulated: 100 Mbps, 200 Mbps, 500 Mbps, 1 Gbps.
- Traffic shapes: steady (Poisson mean=50 qps), microburst (base 20 qps with spikes to 200 qps for 500ms every 30s), conversational session (bursty-turns with long tails).
- Measurement: 30-minute runs per condition after a 10-minute warmup; report p50/p95 latency (ms) and incremental cost estimate ($ per 1k tokens) from our cost model (GPU time + amortized slot cost).

Scenarios tested:
1) steady-50qps / small-batch / prefetch off
2) steady-50qps / small-batch / prefetch on
3) microburst / medium-batch / prefetch off
4) microburst / medium-batch / prefetch on
5) session-bursty / large-batch / prefetch on

Results (aggregated table):
Scenario | Net | p50(ms) | p95(ms) | cost($/1k tokens)
-----------------------------------------------
steady-50 / 100Mbps | 100 Mbps | 48 | 154 | 0.90
steady-50 / 200Mbps | 200 Mbps | 46 | 150 | 0.86
steady-50 / 500Mbps | 500 Mbps | 45 | 148 | 0.85
steady-50 / 1Gbps   | 1 Gbps   | 45 | 147 | 0.85

microburst / 100Mbps | 100 Mbps | 60 | 420 | 1.15
microburst / 200Mbps | 200 Mbps | 58 | 360 | 1.10
microburst / 500Mbps | 500 Mbps | 56 | 310 | 1.09
microburst / 1Gbps   | 1 Gbps   | 54 | 300 | 1.12

session-bursty / 200Mbps | 200 Mbps | 52 | 210 | 0.98
session-bursty / 1Gbps   | 1 Gbps   | 50 | 185 | 1.05

Notes on table: cost values are normalized to our internal 1k-token unit (includes amortized slot + GPU time + incremental networking). The microburst 1Gbps run shows slightly higher cost than 500Mbps because faster responses reduced batching depth and increased per-request overhead in our pricing model.

Textual charts / visualizations (ASCII)
1) p95 vs bandwidth for microburst (lower is better):
 Bandwidth -> p95(ms)
 100Mbps : ################################################ (420)
 200Mbps : ########################################## (360)
 500Mbps : ############################### (310)
 1Gbps   : ############################# (300)

2) cost vs bandwidth for steady-50 (lower is better):
 100Mbps : $0.90 | #####
 200Mbps : $0.86 | ####
 500Mbps : $0.85 | ####
 1Gbps   : $0.85 | ####

3) tradeoff sparkline (p95 normalized 0–1) vs cost normalized 0–1 (session-bursty):
 p95_norm:  |0.95|0.85|0.75|0.68|  (100,200,500,1g)
 cost_norm: |0.90|0.86|0.85|0.88|  (100,200,500,1g)
Interpretation: modest p95 improvements require non-trivial cost or runtime tuning; best ROI observed when enabling prefetch rather than upgrading bandwidth alone.

Observations and rough recommendations (working):
- For most steady production workloads, invest first in runtime features (prefetch, KV hit improvements, smaller latency-targeted batching) rather than network egress upgrades.
- For customers with frequent sub-second microbursts, offer an option: "burst network profile" (1 Gbps egress + prewarm slots for 10s) as a paid offering — yields meaningful p95 reduction but should be priced to reflect reduced batching.
- Add a console signal: show expected p95 delta if customer toggles prefetch and if they increase egress profile (simulate with current traffic shape). This is a low-effort UX with high value for upsell.
- Re-run subset with A100 under constrained memory-cases; early signals show A100 slightly worse on burst tails vs H100 (likely slower NVLink aggregate throughput).

Limitations and open questions:
- This is a short-form scan with single model family; results may differ materially for very large context lengths (>2048 tokens) where I/O to/from KV cache increases.
- Network simulation did not include real-world jitter/packet loss; next iteration should include 1% and 5% packet-drop experiments to test retransmit effects on p95.
- Cost model used internal amortization; share with finance to sanity-check external pricing mapping.

Action items (owner assignments):
- Diego: expand runs to 2 additional models (Llama 13B quantized, an LLM-mix small LLM) and add packet-loss sweeps. target: 2028-11-30.
- Priya: mock console simulation UI (toggle prefetch/egress) and a short A/B text for sales. target: 2028-11-22.
- Evan: sanity-check cost mapping with finance & update cost lines. target: 2028-11-21.

Appendix: quick run notes (for reproducing)
- run harness: benchmarks/run_rosetta.py --model open-llama-7b-int8 --hw H100 --bandwidth 200mbps --shape microburst --batch-target 32 --prefetch true
- logging: aggregated p95 computed from 30s sliding windows to avoid startup spikes.
- artifact locations: S3://redwood-bench/bandwidth-rosetta/2028-11-02/ (raw traces), plot notebook: github.com/redwood-internal/notebooks/bandwidth-rosetta.ipynb

End of draft.

(Notes to self: this reads like a product sell-snapshot; keep language punchy and keep the next iteration focused on packet-loss+jitter and long-context cases.)
